claim: a federation SETTINGS_SYNC push only ever writes the sender's real, persisted settings -- never a transient in-memory overlay

evidence: routes/federation.py's SETTINGS_SYNC receive handler (~508-524) and the /api/federation/settings/sync send handler (~131-137) both build their delta from _load_settings() -- which returns _apply_offline_routing_overlay(_load_settings_raw()). That overlay's own docstring (core/__init__.py:2247-2254) states explicitly: 'Never persisted -- _save_settings writes from the file/the caller's delta, not from this overlaid dict.' Both federation call sites violate that invariant: model_routing (containing the overlay's transient mode:local_only/fallback_to_cloud:False when the sending device is offline) is in _SYNC_SAFE_KEYS and _DEEP_MERGED_BLOCKS, so it gets merged straight into the RECEIVING peer's persisted settings.json. A device that is WAN-offline but still LAN-reachable to a federation peer would silently and permanently rewrite that peer's real model_routing settings on any sync, and would itself broadcast its own transient offline state to every peer. claim: an MCP server subprocess's stdout/stderr cannot be used to grow Friday's memory unboundedly
verdict: BROKEN, FIXED
evidence: MCPServerProcess._read_loop()/_drain_stderr() (mcp_client.py) iterated stdout/stderr via plain `for raw in proc.stdout:` -- Python's line iteration has no per-line size cap, so a malicious or buggy MCP server that never emits a newline (or sends one enormous JSON-RPC line) gets read into a single, unboundedly large Python string. The existing deque(maxlen=40) on _stderr_tail only bounds how many COMPLETED lines are retained, not the size of the one being assembled. Independent of and not mitigated by extension_security.gate_mcp_config()'s destructive-command scan, which checks what the launch command is, not what the running process later writes.
fix_note: Switched both loops to bounded readline(_MAX_LINE_CHARS) (16 MiB, generously larger than any real JSON-RPC message this protocol sends), discarding and resyncing on an oversized frame rather than materializing it. Probe: tests/gauntlet/test_mcp_stdio_line_size_bounded.py (a fake stdout stream distinguishing bounded readline() calls from unbounded bare iteration), proven red->green->red-on-revert. CORRECTION (2026-09-04, flagged by Stephen's independent cold re-verification): the original probe pinned that readline() was CALLED with a bounded size argument -- a proxy for the real property, not the property itself (a caller could pass a bound and still concatenate/hold an unbounded result) -- and covered only _read_loop (stdout); _drain_stderr, the second function this same finding names, had no test at all. Rewritten to assert directly on the length of every string actually RETURNED by readline() during the loop (the real memory-bound property) and to add the identical pair of tests (memory-bound + liveness) for _drain_stderr. Re-verified red->green->red-on-revert against the true pre-fix commit (f4af37a^): both new memory-bound assertions (stdout and stderr) fail cleanly against the reverted bare-iteration code, and the liveness tests still pass (the loop still terminates either way) -- all 4 pass against the fix.

claim: F31's fix_note (this session, earlier tonight): a chunk skipped by MAX_CLOUD_EXTRACT_CALLS 'stays stale in the manifest -- the next delta pass picks it back up' -- implying no chunk is ever permanently lost, only deferred.
verdict: PARTIALLY BROKEN -- true for single-chunk sources, false for multi-chunk ones, FIXED
evidence: KnowledgeGraphManifest.record() (store.py:248-258) keys by source_path, not by chunk id, and OVERWRITES the whole entry on each call rather than merging. In reindex_tier_b's extraction loop, manifest.record(chunk['source_path'], ...) is called only on a chunk's successful extraction -- a cap-skipped chunk (skipped_cloud_cap += 1; continue) never reaches it. But if ANY OTHER chunk from the SAME source file succeeds in the same pass (a wiki page or SOUL.md over CHUNK_SIZE=1200 chars produces multiple chunks via _chunk_text), that chunk's own record() call marks the ENTIRE FILE 'up to date' via its current on-disk fingerprint. The next delta pass's manifest.delta() compares that same current fingerprint, finds no change, classifies the file 'unchanged', and excludes it from `todo` entirely -- so the cap-skipped chunk(s) from that file are never retried, never counted as a failure, and never visible anywhere, unless the file is edited again. Only reachable in gated_cloud mode with a backlog large enough to hit the cap mid-file; local_only (the default) is unaffected since every chunk there is pinned=True and the cap never applies.
found_by: fresh-context sweep agent, knowledge graph seam's 5th verification round (checking F31's own fix for side effects)
fix_note: reindex_tier_b now tracks, per pass, which source_paths had at least one chunk skipped by MAX_CLOUD_EXTRACT_CALLS (capped_sources, a set of canonical() paths, populated at the same point skipped_cloud_cap increments). After the per-chunk extraction loop and before manifest.save(), every capped source_path has manifest.forget() called on it -- unconditionally undoing any manifest.record() a sibling chunk from the SAME file may already have written earlier in the same pass. A capped file's fingerprint is therefore never left 'up to date': the next delta pass sees no manifest entry for it ('new', not 'unchanged'), and ALL of the file's chunks -- not just the ones the cap skipped -- are re-attempted, which is safe because entity merging is idempotent by title (_ent_id). manifest.forget() is a no-op when nothing was recorded for that path this pass, so a file that gets fully capped (no sibling chunk ever succeeded) is unaffected either way. Proof: tests/gauntlet/test_kg_manifest_cap_skip_not_marked_done.py -- the core regression (a 2-chunk file, cap=1: chunk 0 succeeds and would normally record the file done, chunk 1 is capped; asserts the file's canonical path is NOT in the manifest afterward), a full behavioral round-trip (delta pass 1 with cap=1 leaves the file stale; delta pass 2 with the cap lifted re-extracts BOTH chunks, proving the whole file -- not just the capped chunk -- stayed todo), plus two no-op sanity checks (an uncapped multi-chunk file is recorded normally; local_only mode, where the cap never engages, is unaffected). The frontend does nothing to prevent this either: list_schedules() already exposes r['running'] = r.get('id') in _RUNNING, but the live 'Run Now' button (index.html) has no disabled state tied to it at all -- the data needed to prevent the double-click exists and is simply never consulted. Separately, and worse: the scheduler's own nightly 'knowledge_graph_reindex' builtin task calls run_nightly_reindex() -> wiki_graph.rebuild_tier_a() / indexer.reindex_tier_b() DIRECTLY, acquiring neither the _rebuild_lock nor checking _TIER_B_STATE that routes/knowledge_graph.py's manual reindex route uses -- so a user who clicks 'Reindex now' in the Knowledge Graph panel while the 03:30 nightly schedule (or its own Run Now) is mid-run gets two fully concurrent, uncoordinated rebuilds of the same on-disk KG store, because the lock that exists never reaches the code path the scheduler actually uses.

evidence: tests/conftest.py line 38 (pre-fix): _TEST_HOME = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="friday_test_home_")) at module import time, with no matching cleanup anywhere in the file, no pytest_sessionfinish hook, no fixture finalizer. Two mechanisms, both in tests/conftest.py. (1) pytest_sessionfinish(session, exitstatus) now shutil.rmtree(_TEST_HOME, ignore_errors=True) on every normal exit -- a suite that runs to completion leaks nothing at all. (2) _sweep_stale_test_homes(base, max_age_seconds=3600), called once at collection time before the new _TEST_HOME is created, removes any friday_test_home_* directory older than the threshold -- this is what reclaims space from a run that never reaches the sessionfinish hook (Ctrl+C, OOM kill, a hard crash), which is exactly the failure mode that let 3,858 directories accumulate silently over three months. Bounded to only its own prefix (never touches unrelated temp-dir siblings) and wrapped in ignore_errors/except OSError throughout so a locked file on Windows cannot fail an actual test run. CORRECTION (2026-09-04, same day, hours later): this fix was ALSO STILL LEAKING in real use. Stephen measured it directly -- after the verifier's cleanup freed ~153GB, C: dropped from ~200GB to 138GB free in about an hour (~60GB/hour), on pace to refill and crash the live app again within roughly two hours. His diagnosis requirement was explicit: prove it 'the usual way -- a run that leaves nothing behind, verified by counting the directories before and after rather than by reading the fixture' -- and a direct before/after count of tests/gauntlet/test_conftest_temp_home_cleanup.py's own run confirmed a real, deterministic +1 leak that the isolated-function test (which calls pytest_sessionfinish/‌_sweep_stale_test_homes directly against tmp_path fixtures, never a real pytest process) could not see.

ROOT CAUSE, the real and dominant one: this file's OWN docstring already documented, as a known quirk, that 'pytest imports this file as conftest, so a test doing `from tests.conftest import ...` executes the module a SECOND time' -- but only the OTHER env vars in the file were guarded against that with os.environ.setdefault(); _TEST_HOME creation itself used a hard `=`, so every second execution minted a genuinely new, real tempfile.mkdtemp() directory that pytest's plugin system never knew about (only the FIRST, pytest-registered module instance's pytest_sessionfinish is ever actually invoked -- a second plain `import` doesn't register a second plugin). Confirmed the blast radius is not a rare edge case: tests/api/conftest.py -- loaded automatically for EVERY test under tests/api/ -- does exactly `from tests.conftest import CANNED_TEXT`, and tests/fake_backends.py does the same, so this fires on effectively every historical `pytest tests/unit tests/api` run, the exact command this file's own docstring recommends as 'Run everything.' This is almost certainly the dominant mechanism behind the 3,858-directory historical accumulation, not primarily a rare Windows file-lock race (a real but secondary risk, addressed separately below).

REAL FIX: _TEST_HOME creation is now guarded by a PID-tagged idempotency check (`_FRIDAY_TEST_HOME` env var storing `f'{os.getpid()}:{path}'`) -- a second execution in the SAME process reuses the first execution's _TEST_HOME instead of minting a new untracked one. The PID tag matters specifically because this env var is inherited by any subprocess a test spawns (e.g. the new end-to-end probe below, which shells out to a real `pytest` invocation) -- without it, a CHILD process would see its PARENT's already-set env var and wrongly reuse the STILL-IN-USE parent directory instead of creating its own, which would be worse than the leak (the child's own sessionfinish would eventually rmtree a directory the parent is actively using). Verified directly, outside any assertion, that parent and child get genuinely different homes despite the inherited env var. Also hardened pytest_sessionfinish's OWN rmtree with a short retry-with-backoff (0, 50ms, 100ms, 200ms, 400ms) before falling back to best-effort, for the secondary, real-but-rarer Windows-file-lock scenario (a logging.FileHandler or open sqlite connection still momentarily held at the exact instant of session teardown, which a single-shot ignore_errors=True rmtree can silently leave behind with zero trace).

claim: memory_rollback(timestamp) restores each affected key to whatever value it held before timestamp, as its name and original docstring claimed ("Roll back all writes that occurred after timestamp")
verdict: BROKEN, confirmed by direct execution, not just reading. write_memory() keeps no per-key version history at all -- a second write to the same key unconditionally overwrites the first's on-disk {key}.json file, with nothing anywhere retaining the earlier value. By the time memory_rollback() runs, the ONLY on-disk copy of a rolled-back key is whatever the LATEST write left there -- never the value it held before the cutoff. Reproduced the reviewer's exact scenario: write_memory('k','A'), record a cutoff, write_memory('k','B'), then memory_rollback(cutoff) -- read_memory('k') afterward returns None. Not 'A' (the pre-cutoff value), not 'B' (the post-cutoff value): the key is gone entirely, because the file rollback moved out of place held 'B', and 'A' had already been destroyed the instant 'B' was written, independent of rollback ever running. A repo-wide grep for the exact local variable name `rollback_dir` (unique to memory_rollback's own implementation) confirms nothing anywhere in src/agent_friday/ ever reads the `_rollback/<cutoff>/` directory files are moved into -- so there is no restoration path of any kind, automated or otherwise, once a key is rolled back. Reachable today via a real, @login_required route (POST /api/memory/rollback, routes/insights.py) -- no UI currently calls it, but the backend accepts the call from anyone already authenticated.
evidence: Direct execution via an isolated CognitiveMemory(memory_dir=<tmp>) instance (never touching the real ~/.friday/memory): write_memory('k','A') -> sleep -> cutoff=time.time() -> sleep -> write_memory('k','B') -> read_memory('k') returns 'B' (confirms the overwrite-in-place behavior) -> memory_rollback(cutoff) -> read_memory('k') returns None. 4 pinning tests added at tests/gauntlet/test_cognitive_memory_rollback_does_not_restore.py, all passing: (1) the exact write-A/write-B/rollback reproduction above, (2) a key written only after the cutoff is correctly removed (the one case rollback genuinely handles right, since nonexistent IS the correct pre-cutoff state -- named explicitly as the falsifiability/grounding case), (3) a key never touched after the cutoff is correctly left alone, (4) a git-grep structural check that nothing outside cognitive_memory.py itself references the `rollback_dir` local variable name, grounding the 'nothing reads it back' claim against future silent changes.

claim: run_epoch() only promotes a candidate skill version to become the new champion when there is genuine evaluation signal backing that decision
verdict: BROKEN, confirmed by direct execution of all four scenarios the review asked to be reproduced (it had only inspected the source, explicitly flagged for verification-by-execution before trusting it). Mechanism: composite_score() treats a metrics dict with no latency_ms/cost_usd keys as PERFECT on those two dimensions (normalize_latency/normalize_cost both return 1.0 for an absent/zero value, meant for 'fast and cheap', not 'unknown') -- so any degenerate fallback metrics dict of just {"accuracy": 0.0} scores exactly 0.25 under default weights (0.15 latency + 0.10 cost, both maxed), not 0.0 as the accuracy-only intent would suggest. Three independent paths through run_epoch() collapse BOTH candidate_score and baseline_score to this exact same 0.25 fallback value, producing an artificial tie: (1) the evaluator raises an exception on every case in the batch, (2) no evaluator is configured at all and neither candidate nor baseline has any prior execution history, (3) eval_batch is empty (candidate_score=baseline_score=0.0 in this specific sub-case, also a tie). ValidationGate.evaluate()'s own tolerance rule then treats ANY tie (candidate_score >= baseline_score, improvement < 0.005) as a 'marginal pass', so all three promote. A control case with a real, working evaluator that finds a genuine regression is correctly rejected -- confirming the gate mechanism itself is sound; the defect is specifically that total failure/absence of signal is indistinguishable from a confirmed, genuine tie. Separately confirmed: epoch.reason recorded the evaluator's actual exception message inside the per-case loop, then was unconditionally overwritten afterward by the gate's own reason string, silently discarding the diagnostic -- so even a human reading a promoted/rejected epoch's own reason field had no way to see that the evaluator had been failing. Reachability, for honest severity: as of this fix, SkillOptEngine.run_epoch() is not reachable from any live production path -- no Flask route calls it (routes/skills.py only exposes a read-only GET /api/skillopt/state), no CLI subcommand calls it (skillopt_engine.py's _cli_main only has status/show/versions/export/register), and the currently-wired nightly pipeline (skill_capture.run_nightly() -> maybe_autoresearch() -> AutoResearchLoop.maybe_trigger()) never calls it either -- AutoResearchLoop's own docstring documents run_epoch as pipeline step 5 ("Hand candidates to TrainingEpoch -- validation gate decides"), but apply_finding() stops after registering a new candidate version, never actually invoking it. The one production instantiation (get_engine()'s singleton) constructs SkillOptEngine() with zero arguments, so evaluator is always None in the only place this could currently run at all -- exactly the worst-case input this bug mishandled. Fixed now, before that documented-but-missing wiring lands.
evidence: Reproduction script executed 4 scenarios against an isolated SkillOptEngine(root=<tmp>): (1) evaluator raising RuntimeError on every case -> pre-fix: decision='promoted', both scores 0.25 identical; (2) no evaluator, fresh never-executed candidate+baseline -> pre-fix: decision='promoted', both scores 0.25; (3) empty eval_batch -> pre-fix: decision='promoted', both scores 0.0; (4) control, a real evaluator correctly finding a regression -> decision='rejected' both before and after the fix (unaffected, confirms the gate itself works given real signal). Post-fix, scenarios 1-3 all changed to decision='inconclusive' with a reason naming why (the actual exception message preserved verbatim for scenario 1). Red-on-revert proven via git-stash-isolated revert of only skillopt_engine.py's run_epoch() change: 5 of 7 new tests in tests/gauntlet/test_skillopt_run_epoch_promotion_requires_signal.py failed against the pre-fix code (the 2 that stayed green are the non-regression control cases exercising pre-existing correct gate behavior, unaffected by this change) -- fix re-applied, all 7 green. Full existing suite (tests/unit/test_skillopt_engine.py, tests/unit/test_learning_loop.py, tests/unit/test_learning_loop_lifecycle.py, tests/api/test_skillopt_llm_research.py, tests/gauntlet/) reran clean after the fix, 493 tests, zero failures.
fix_note: src/agent_friday/skillopt_engine.py, run_epoch(): track successful_cases (an evaluator call that didn't raise, or -- in the no-evaluator path -- both candidate and baseline genuinely having prior accuracy history rather than a defaulted 0.0) and eval_errors (the exception messages) alongside the existing per-case loop. After the loop: an empty eval_batch, or zero successful_cases across a non-empty batch, now short-circuits to decision='inconclusive' with a reason naming the cause, returning BEFORE the gate or _promote() are ever reached -- completing a decision state ('pending | promoted | rejected | inconclusive') the TrainingEpoch dataclass's own field comment already declared but run_epoch() never actually produced. A PARTIAL failure (some cases evaluated, some didn't) still proceeds to the gate exactly as before -- deliberately not forced inconclusive, since some real signal exists -- but the reason string now always names the failure count and the last error instead of being silently dropped. Did not touch ValidationGate.evaluate()'s tie-tolerance policy itself (a real, working evaluator's genuine tie or marginal improvement still passes, per existing design) -- only the specific defect of failure/absence being indistinguishable from a genuine tie.
note: composite_score()'s own latency/cost defaulting (absent reads as 'perfect', not 'unknown') is the specific mechanism that produced the 0.25 floor value both broken paths collapsed to -- left as-is here since it is shared, working-as-designed behavior for the normal case (a real caller who simply doesn't care about latency/cost for a given skill), and the run_epoch()-level fix (refuse to promote on zero signal, regardless of what fallback value the gate would have seen) fully closes the promotion-on-failure gap without needing to touch that shared scoring primitive.

claim: _success_score() verifies that a chat turn actually accomplished what the reply claims before scoring it a success
verdict: CONFIRMED, real and severe, matching the reviewer's own reported example exactly.
